title: Longest Mountain in Array
statement:
A **mountain** is a sequence of at least 3 numbers that rises strictly to a single peak and then falls strictly to its last number: there is a peak position `p`, neither the first nor the last position, such that every number before `p` is smaller than the one after it, and every number from `p` onward is larger than the one after it. Equal neighbours break a mountain.

Given the integer array `arr`, return the length of the longest contiguous subarray of `arr` that is a mountain, or `0` when no subarray is one.
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every subarray for the mountain shape costs O(n³). But mountains never overlap in a useful way: once a climb and its descent are walked, the next mountain can only start where this one ended (the bottom of a descent can be the base of the next climb). So one pointer `start` marks a possible left base and a second pointer `end` walks up and then down from it; neither pointer ever moves back.

## Approach

1. Set `best = 0` and `start = 0`.
2. From `start`, set `end = start`. If the next number is larger, a climb begins: move `end` while the numbers keep rising.
3. If `end` is now followed by a smaller number, it is a peak: move `end` while the numbers keep falling, then record `end - start + 1` in `best`.
4. Jump `start` to `end` (the bottom of the descent may start the next climb), or one step forward when `end` did not move.
5. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [2, 1, 4, 7, 3, 2, 5]`. At `start = 0` the next number `1` is smaller, so no climb; `start` becomes 1. From index 1 the values rise `1, 4, 7` (`end = 3`), then fall `7, 3, 2` (`end = 5`), so `best = 5 - 1 + 1 = 5`. `start` jumps to 5; the climb `2, 5` reaches the end of the array with no descent, so nothing is recorded. The answer is `5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): `end` never moves backward and `start` only jumps forward.
- Space: O(1): a few indices.

## Pitfalls

- A climb with no descent (or a descent with no climb) is not a mountain; record a length only after both parts exist.
- Equal neighbours stop both the climb and the descent, so a flat top is never a peak.
- Set `start` to `end`, not `end + 1`: the last number of a descent is also the first number of the next climb.
- Always advance `start` by at least one, or the loop never ends on flat or falling stretches.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `arr` |
| `best` | longest mountain length found so far |
| `start` | left base of the mountain being tried |
| `end` | pointer that walks up the climb and down the descent |

narration.3: No mountain has been seen yet, so the best length starts at 0.
narration.4: The first possible left base is index 0.
narration.6: Keep trying left bases until start runs off the array.
narration.7: The second pointer end begins at the base and will walk the mountain.
narration.8: A mountain can only start here if the next number is larger.
narration.9: Climb while each number is smaller than the one after it.
narration.10: Move end one step up the slope.
narration.12: After the climb, end is a peak only if the next number is smaller.
narration.13: Descend while each number is larger than the one after it.
narration.14: Move end one step down the slope.
narration.16: Both a climb and a descent exist, so start..end is a mountain; keep the longer length.
narration.19: The bottom of this descent can be the base of the next climb, so jump start to end, but always move forward at least one step.
narration.21: Every base was tried; return the longest mountain length.
